question: Naive string matching checks a pattern P of length m against a text T of length n by trying all n-m+1 positions. Worst-case time complexity?
options: quadratic time in n and m
explanation: Each position requires O(m) character comparisons; n-m+1 positions means O(n*m) quadratic time in worst case.

question: Knuth-Morris-Pratt (KMP) algorithm preprocesses a pattern to build a failure function (LPS array) allowing O(n+m) matching time. What does LPS represent?
options: longest proper prefix which is also suffix
explanation: LPS[i] stores the length of the longest proper prefix of P[0..i] that is also a suffix, enabling intelligent skipping of failed matches.

question: Boyer-Moore algorithm for string matching skips characters using a bad-character rule (furthest right occurrence of a character in pattern). Why does this speed up matching?
options: mismatches can skip multiple characters instead of one
explanation: When a mismatch occurs, the bad-character rule skips based on the mismatched text character, potentially jumping multiple positions.

question: Rabin-Karp algorithm uses polynomial rolling hash to match patterns. A hash collision occurs when two different substrings hash to the same value. What is the risk?
options: false positives require confirming actual match
explanation: Hash collisions are false positives; must verify the actual characters; real matches are never missed (no false negatives).

question: Rabin-Karp hashing of a substring takes O(m) to compute initially but O(1) to update when sliding one character. How is O(1) update achieved?
options: by computing rolling hash: remove leftmost contribution and add new character
explanation: Rolling hash: subtract old character's contribution, shift, add new character; each operation is constant-time arithmetic.

question: Using regular expressions for pattern matching is powerful but potentially slow. Why do engines using backtracking have worst-case exponential time for certain patterns?
options: alternation and quantifiers can cause exponential state exploration
explanation: Patterns like (a+)+ matching a string of a's cause backtracking to explore all possible splits, creating exponential time in input length.

question: Aho-Corasick algorithm finds multiple pattern matches in text simultaneously. Compared to running KMP separately for each pattern, what is the advantage?
options: Aho-Corasick builds a trie once and scans text once: O(n+m+z) vs O(n*k) for k patterns
explanation: Aho-Corasick uses a finite automaton built from all patterns; scanning text is O(n) once; total is O(n+m+z) where z is match count.

question: Z-algorithm computes an array Z where Z[i] is the length of the longest substring starting at i matching a prefix of the string. Time complexity?
explanation: Z-algorithm scans the string once, maintaining a window of matched prefix; each character is processed once, giving O(n) linear time.

question: Suffix array and suffix tree are used for efficient pattern matching on a static text. Suffix array requires O(n log n) space and O(log n) per pattern query. Why is suffix array preferred over naive search for many queries?
options: suffix array amortizes preprocessing; with many queries, O((n log n + q log n) < O(n*m*q)
suffix array uses less space always
explanation: Suffix array preprocessing is O(n log n) once; q queries are O(log n) each; total O((n + q) log n) beats O(n*m*q) naive for large q.

question: Wildcard pattern matching where '?' matches any single character and '*' matches any sequence: naive backtracking can be exponential. What DP approach solves it in O(n*m) time?
options: dp[i][j] represents if T[0..i-1] matches P[0..j-1]
explanation: dp[i][j] tracks matches; transitions handle literals, '?', and '*'; filling the (n+1) x (m+1) table is O(n*m) time.
